summary: Correct parts and proportions (1.5 m white pole, top cap, exposed spring, ground socket, sleeved flag), but the flag cloth looks like a frozen rigid sheet and the materials are clean and flat.
critique: Silhouette and scale read correctly: pole about 1.5 m, flag roughly 450-500 mm square, cap on top, black collars above and below a coil spring, and a socket plate at turf level. The spring is a real coil with highlights, which is the best detail here. What breaks realism: (1) The flag sticks out from the pole at full width with a few even sine-wave folds, as if starched, and does not sag under gravity. In still air a corner flag hangs limp against the pole, and in wind it flutters with a diagonal twist and a curled free edge. This even horizontal wave is the classic CG-flag look. (2) The cloth is a flat lemon yellow with no weave, no hem stitching on the free edges and no difference in light between the back and front. Real nylon corner flags are a saturated fluorescent yellow (about sRGB 235,230,40) with a double-stitched hem and slight translucency when backlit. (3) The pole is a plain smooth grey-white cylinder with uniform roughness. It has no scuffs, grass stains or mud splash on the bottom 200 mm, no moulded joint where the pole meets the spring adaptor, and no decal or maker band. (4) The brown disc around the socket reads as a mud mat or a cork coaster. Real pro sockets are either a flush black plastic sleeve cap of about 60-70 mm diameter set into the turf, or a weighted rubber base about 300 mm across and dark grey or black. (5) The flag sleeve wraps the pole only as a slightly offset tube. It has no visible ties or clips at the top and bottom, which pro flags have.
suggestions: Re-pose the flag cloth: give it 2-3 static variants (limp, light breeze, wind), each about 12x12 quads (~300 tris), with gravity sag so the free bottom corner drops 80-150 mm below the top edge, a diagonal twist and a curled free edge. Pick a variant per instance, or drive a cheap vertex-shader flutter from vertex colour (weight 0 at the sleeve, 1 at the free edge).

Flag material: saturated fluorescent yellow albedo (~0.92,0.90,0.16 linear-ish), roughness 0.65, plus a tileable 256 px nylon weave normal map and a 15 mm stitched hem strip (darker, 2-px stitch line) on the three free edges. Add 0.2-0.3 transmission or a back-face lighten hack so it glows when backlit.

Replace the brown disc with a flush black socket cap (Ø 70 mm, 5 mm proud, roughness 0.5) or a dark rubber weighted base (Ø 300 mm, 40 mm tall with a chamfer). Blend the turf contact with a small decal of darker flattened grass, not a brown plate.

Pole wear: vertex-colour or a 128x512 strip texture with grass stain and mud on the lowest 250 mm, a few hairline scuffs, and roughness varying 0.35-0.55. Add a 20 mm moulded transition collar where the pole enters the spring adaptor.
Add two small sleeve ties (8-tri boxes) at the top and bottom of the flag sleeve, and a slightly domed top cap with a parting line.
Total budget stays under ~800 tris plus one shared 256-512 px atlas, so it remains trivially instanceable.
renderer_notes: The lawn is a renderer/ground asset. The hard dark shadow of the flag is correct for a single sun.

summary: Correct UK 8-yard skip form (vertical sides, raked ends, lugs, stencilled hire lettering, hazard chevrons, rubble load), let down by polka-dot rust, pristine flat panels and a load that reads as a textured mound.
critique: Good: the size is right for an 8-yard skip (about 3.4-3.6 m long at the top, 1.7 m wide, 1.2 m high). The long sides are vertical and the ends raked, there are vertical stiffening channels, four chain-lift lugs on the long sides plus lugs on the ends, red/white chevron boards on the end, a drop-door with locking bars, and stencilled operator name and phone number. The load mixes bricks, blocks, timber and a black sack. Problems: (1) The rust is evenly sprinkled round dots across every panel at the same density, which looks like a pattern applied to a clean object. Real skip wear is concentrated: the top rim is scraped to bare grey and orange steel from the grab and bucket, there are vertical scrape streaks down the outside from being dragged on and off the lorry, rust bleeds from welds and lug plates, and impact dents cluster on the lower corners and ends. Large areas of yellow should stay intact but faded and chalky. (2) The panels are perfectly flat. Real skips are visibly battered, with dished side panels, dented rims and bent channels. (3) The lettering wear removes whole letters ('BRAM EY', 'SKIP  RE') at random, which reads as a bug rather than wear. Real stencil wear is partial: scuffed through the paint, with edges intact. (4) The rim is a thin square yellow strip. Real skips have a heavy top rail of about 100x100 mm box or rolled section, darker with grime. (5) The interior is a flat rust colour with no scrape marks. (6) The rubble is a low displaced mound with a noisy grey texture, and the bricks and blocks are uniform clean cubes. The black sack is too glossy and smooth, like a pebble. Nothing sticks up past the rim (a plank or a bit of plasterboard), and there is no dust. (7) There is no dirt, mud or dust on the lower third, the lettering is very crisp, and there is no fresh paint over old operator lettering.
suggestions: Replace the uniform rust dots with a masked wear system in one 1024 px trim/atlas: a scraped bare-steel band 30-80 mm along the whole top rim, vertical drag streaks on the lower 400 mm of the sides, rust runs below each lug and weld seam, and chipped-paint clusters only at corners and edges. Keep 70%+ of the yellow intact but desaturated (albedo ~0.55,0.42,0.05, roughness 0.7).

Deform the mesh: dish each side panel inward 20-40 mm between the stiffening channels, add 3-5 dents at the lower corners and ends (vertex push), and give the rim a slight random wave of ±15 mm. All of this is free in vertex count if the panels are split into a 4x3 grid (~+200 tris).
Make the top rim a proper 100x100 mm box section with a 10 mm bevel, and add a small lip on the inner face, so the rim catches a highlight line.

Lettering wear: keep every glyph and erode it with a noise mask (20-40% coverage, more at the bottom), never removing whole letters. Optionally show the ghost of an older operator's lettering under a repaint patch in a slightly different yellow.

Rubble: build the mound from 3-4 overlapping lumpy meshes with height variation of 300-500 mm, scatter 20-40 instanced debris pieces (broken bricks with chipped corners, half blocks, a bent pipe, a plasterboard sheet, a pallet slat) with a few poking out above the rim at angles, use a matte dull black for the bag (roughness 0.45, crinkle normal map), and add a dust overlay on everything (albedo lift, roughness 0.9).
Add a grime gradient (darker, browner, rougher) on the bottom 300 mm outside, plus mud on the base runners, and a soft contact-shadow decal under the skip.
Budget: ~2.5-4k tris for the skip with load, one 1024 atlas plus a shared rubble atlas. Fine for scattering.
renderer_notes: The end view makes the skip look slightly lifted because of the shadow offset and no ambient occlusion at the runners. A baked AO/contact decal would fix the impression.

summary: Recognisable 13 t crawler excavator with cab, counterweight, handrails, beacon and hoses, but the boom/arm geometry is wrong (no arm cylinder on top of the boom, arm hanging vertically), the cylinders are spindly, and it is showroom-clean.
critique: Overall size and the house/undercarriage ratio are about right for a 313-class machine (about 2.5 m wide, cab left, boom centre-right, rounded counterweight, exhaust stack, engine-hood grille, mirrors, beacon, rails, decals 'EX135' and 'TERRADIG'). Problems, in order of how much they hurt: (1) Front linkage. Real excavators have a single large arm (stick) cylinder on top of the boom, running from a boss near the boom foot to the top of the stick behind the boom-nose pin. Here there is no arm cylinder at all, only black hose lines along the boom top, so it is not clear what holds the stick. The stick hangs perfectly vertical, which is an unnatural rest pose. The boom's rounded-arch shape is too even, like a bent tube. A real boom is a welded box with a sharp 'banana' kink, flat side plates, and deep reinforcing plates and a heavy casting at the nose. (2) The cylinders are thin pencils. Boom cylinders on a 13 t machine are about 120-140 mm barrel diameter and the bucket cylinder about 100 mm, with visible gland nuts and grease nipples. The bucket linkage (H-link and dogbone) is crude black bars. (3) The bucket is a closed box with teeth stuck on its outside face. Real buckets have a curved wrap plate, a cutting lip with 4-5 adapter-mounted teeth, side cutters and wear strips. The bucket and teeth should be worn to bare steel and covered in dirt. (4) Undercarriage: the track loops and grousers are OK, but there are no lower track rollers, no upper carrier roller visible, no recoil guard, and the track frame is a flat dark slab. The sprocket/idler detail is minimal. (5) Materials: uniform clean CAT-ish yellow with slight smudges. There is no mud on the tracks or lower body, no hydraulic oil stains, no scraped paint on the bucket, stick or counterweight corners, and no exhaust soot on the hood. Glass is OK, with a seat inside. (6) Small things: the counterweight has no lifting eyes or reflective chevrons beyond one small decal, the handrails are thin, and there are no steps on the track frame.
suggestions: Fix the linkage first: add an arm cylinder (barrel Ø 130 mm, ~1.6 m long) on top of the boom, from a boss about 1/3 along the boom to a clevis on the stick heel about 400 mm above the boom-nose pin. Pose the machine in a believable rest: stick angled 20-30° back toward the cab and bucket curled, resting on the ground, or the classic transport pose.

Rebuild the boom as a box section: two flat side plates with a top and bottom flange, a pronounced kink about 55% along, a foot casting at the house, and a widened nose casting with pin bosses (all pins Ø 70-80 mm with retainer plates). About 600-900 tris.
Thicken all cylinders (boom 2x Ø 130, bucket Ø 110), add gland nuts, rod-eye clevises and a short steel-tube section where the hoses route along the boom, with hose loops at the boom nose.

Bucket: model a curved wrap with side plates, a cutting edge, 4 teeth on adapters and side cutters. Texture it with a bare-steel worn band on the lip and teeth (metallic 1, roughness 0.4), scratched paint and caked dirt inside.

Undercarriage: add 7 lower rollers and 1-2 carrier rollers per side (simple 12-sided cylinders), a sprocket with teeth, an idler with a recoil housing, and a grimy track frame. Apply a mud/dirt vertex-colour gradient to the tracks and lower 400 mm of the house.

Wear pass in a 2048 atlas: edge chipping on the counterweight corners and hood edges, oil weep below the cylinder glands, soot around the exhaust, faded/chalky paint on the upper surfaces, plus anti-slip tread on the walkway tops and a safety chevron set on the counterweight.
Budget target ~15-25k tris LOD0 with a 2048 atlas, and LOD1 at ~5k. Fine for a few instances per construction site.
renderer_notes: No AO makes the gap between the house and the tracks read lighter than it should. The flat lawn hides the lack of mud, but the asset itself still needs dirt.

summary: Clean, correctly sized 32-panel classic ball with subtle sheen, scuffs and a small 'PRO MATCH SIZE 5' print. It reads well, but the silhouette is a perfect sphere and the seams are painted lines with no depth.
critique: Good: about 220 mm diameter, correct truncated-icosahedron layout, believable glossy PU sheen with soft smudges on the white panels, and an understated stripe logo with legible small text. Problems: (1) The silhouette is a perfect sphere. Stitched balls have slightly pillowed panels with recessed seams, so the outline is subtly faceted and lumpy, and the lighting shows a soft dip at every seam. Here the seams are thin grey lines in the albedo, with almost no normal response, so the ball looks printed. (2) There is no stitch detail at close range (real hand-stitched seams show a row of stitch dimples). Thermo-bonded modern balls would instead show a crisp groove. (3) The black panels are uniformly matte charcoal and the white panels uniformly clean. A used training ball has grass stains, scuffs concentrated on random strike zones, mud in the seams and a slightly yellowed white. (4) The print is small and low-contrast. That is fine for realism, but there is only one logo. Real balls repeat the branding 2-4 times plus a valve with a small printed 'valve' marking or a ring, and the valve is missing.
suggestions: Pillow the panels: subdivide to about 1-1.5k tris and push each panel's interior outward 1.5-2 mm relative to its edges (or bake this into a 1024 normal map from a high-poly). The seams then sit about 1.5 mm into the silhouette and pick up a soft shadow line.
Add a seam normal and AO channel: a 2-3 mm groove with a stitch-dimple pattern every ~4 mm (normal map only), with AO darkening (~0.6) in the groove.
Add a valve: a 6 mm dark rubber dot on one white panel with a 12 mm printed ring.

Make 2-3 material variants: new (current), training-used (grass-green and mud smudges biased to one hemisphere, dirt in seams, white albedo dropped to ~0.75 and warmed), and wet (roughness 0.15, slightly darker). Variants cost only extra 512-1024 textures.
Repeat the logo/branding block on the opposite panel and add a small panel-number or 'FIFA quality'-style certification roundel (generic, no real marks).
renderer_notes: The ball sits on the tips of tall grass cards, so it appears to float slightly. That is the lawn system, not the ball.

summary: Charming period tip-up seat with cast standards, slatted back, brass seat number and rust-streaked bolts, but the wood reads as a regular stripe texture, the slats float off the frame, and the double armrests and proportions feel like a garden chair.
critique: Good: dark green cast-iron standards with flanged feet and bolt holes, a pivot boss for the tip-up pan, a wooden slatted back with carriage-bolt heads and rust streaks below them, and a small brass number plate '23'. All of these are the right vocabulary for an old English terrace or main-stand seat. Problems: (1) The wood grain is an evenly spaced set of parallel stripes (it reads as corduroy or ribbed plastic). There are no knots, end grain, varnish wear on the front edge of the seat or the top of the back, grey weathered timber, or split or checked slat ends. The rear face of the back is a much darker, redder varnish than the front, so it looks like two different woods. (2) The armrest ends show a regular serrated or ribbed profile that reads as a geometry artefact. (3) From the side, the back slats stand off the frame with visible air between slat and standard, as if floating. Real slats sit on the standard's back rail and are through-bolted. (4) In a real row the standards and armrests are shared between neighbouring seats. As a standalone seat this one carries two full armrests and two full standards, so instancing it side by side will double the armrests and look wrong unless a row-module variant exists. (5) The standards are plain extrusions with soft bevels and uniform paint. Old cast seats have ornate or at least moulded profiles, chipped paint showing earlier colour coats, and rust at the foot bolts. (6) The proportions are plausible (seat pivot ~430-450 mm, back top ~900 mm), but the back is tall with 3 wide slats and the tipped-up pan sits so close to the back that from the front the seat reads as one big slatted panel. Real tip-up wooden seats show a clear gap and a visible underside of the pan with its iron hinge brackets.
suggestions: Replace the stripe texture with a real hardwood atlas (1024x256 per slat, 4-6 variants): irregular grain flow, a couple of knots, darker end grain, varnish worn to grey bare timber on the seat front edge and back top rail, and fine checking at slat ends. Use the same species and tone on both faces, with the rear just slightly less worn.
Remove the serrated armrest end profile. Give the armrests a simple rounded end (bevel 6-8 mm) and a worn varnish highlight where hands rest.

Seat the back slats onto the standard: add a 40x10 mm iron back rail on each standard that the slats sit against, with through-bolts at each slat/rail intersection (domed heads already exist), so there is no air gap.
Make it row-modular: split into 'standard with shared armrest' and 'seat bay (pan + back slats)' so rows of N seats use N+1 standards. That halves the frame cost and makes rows look right.
Show the pan underside: a 15-20 mm gap between the tipped pan and the back, two iron hinge brackets under the pan, and a rubber stop bumper on the standard.

Cast-iron material: chipped green paint with older cream/red layers peeking through at edges (layered mask), rust at foot bolts and the pivot, roughness 0.55-0.75. Add a slightly moulded profile to the standard edges (a 5 mm raised rib along the curve).
Budget ~1.2-2k tris per seat bay + standard, sharing one 1024 atlas. Fine for thousands of instances with LOD1 as a few slat boxes.
renderer_notes: Standing alone on long grass exaggerates its garden-chair feel. On a concrete terrace step it would read better.

summary: Right overall size and high-roof L4 Transit-style proportions, but it reads as a clean white block with smooth-shading streaks, missing tail lamps, a front plate and real front-end detail.
critique: Length, height and wheelbase are close to a Ford Transit 17-seat L4 high roof (about 6.7 m long, 2.78 m high, 3.75 m wheelbase), with a high-roof cap, tinted side glazing showing seat backs, rear barn doors with a central seam, a high-level brake light and a rear plate. Problems: (1) The rear has no main tail-lamp clusters. Transits have tall vertical lamp clusters in the rear pillars, and their absence makes the back look like a box. The rear bumper is a thin black strip with no step plate. (2) The front has no number plate, the headlamps are thin flat slivers without lens depth, the grille is a generic slatted plate, and there is no lower bumper intake, fog lamps or tow eye. The bonnet has no shut line and there are no windscreen wipers. (3) The body is a single uniform white with obvious vertical light streaks from shading normals or faceting along the sides. There are no panel shut lines on the bonnet, wings or roof cap, no sliding-door rail outside, no fuel flap detail, and no rubbing strip detail beyond flat black lines. (4) Single rear wheels. Many 17-seat L4 Transits use twin rear wheels (DRW), and if single, the tyres should look bigger and the wheels have proper hub caps. The wheel arches have no liner or depth, so the tyres look painted into the arch. (5) No livery, branding or 'minibus' signage, and no dirt. A training-ground squad bus would usually carry club livery or a hire-company decal and road grime on the lower body. (6) The roof-top amber markers are fine, but the roof has no ribs or AC pod, which are typical on a conversion.
suggestions: Add tail-lamp clusters: two vertical units about 250x700 mm in the rear corner pillars (red/amber/clear lens sections, emissive mask), a rear bumper with a black textured step centre and reflectors. ~300 tris.

Front end: a recessed headlamp housing with clear lens and reflector geometry (or parallax-ish normal map), a lower bumper with intake grille and fog lamps, a front UK plate (white, 520x111 mm), wipers parked on the cowl, and shut lines for the bonnet and wings via a trim normal map.

Fix the side shading: use smoothing groups or split normals at the window-line crease and wheel arches so the large flat panels shade evenly, and bake a subtle panel-ripple normal. Add shut lines for sliding door, cab doors and roof cap, plus an external sliding-door rail at the waistline behind the door.
Wheel arches: model inner arch liners (black, ~60 mm deep) and give each wheel a proper 16-in steel wheel or hub cap with lug nuts. Offer a DRW rear-axle variant for the 17-seater.

Materials: white paint albedo ~0.8 with clearcoat-ish roughness 0.25, a dirt gradient on the lower 400 mm and behind the wheels, slightly lighter roof cap GRP. Add 2-3 livery decal variants (club-colour stripe and crest placeholder, hire-company text) via a single 2048 decal atlas.
Roof: add a low AC pod or roof vents and a subtle GRP seam where the high-roof cap meets the body.
Budget: ~10-15k tris LOD0, one 2048 atlas plus a shared vehicle detail atlas.
renderer_notes: No SSR or reflections makes white paint and black glass look flat. Reflection probes or a sky-cube reflection would help all vehicles, independent of the mesh.

summary: Believable grassroots corner pole (yellow/black banded pole, black rubber foot, chequered flag), but the chequer colour is washed-out salmon, the flag is a starched horizontal sheet, and there are small white dot artefacts and a brown disc base.
critique: Proportions are right: a pole of about 1.5 m, 25-30 mm diameter, with yellow/black banding, a yellow top cap, a black rubber or spring-boot base and a 4x4 chequer flag of about 450 mm square with a sleeve. Problems: (1) The red is salmon/peach (about sRGB 235,120,90) with pinkish shading. Grassroots chequer flags are fluorescent orange or vivid red against white, and should be much more saturated. (2) The flag shape is the same rigid even wave as the pro flag. It does not sag and the free edge does not curl. (3) There are two small white dots near the free edge of the flag (texture or geometry artefacts) that break the chequer. (4) The pole bands are perfectly clean glossy yellow and black with no scuffing, faded yellow, mud splash or grass staining. Grassroots poles are battered: faded, bent slightly, with tape repairs and scratches. (5) The brown disc under the base reads as a coaster or mud mat. A grassroots pole is usually pushed straight into the turf, into a plastic ground sleeve, or into a black rubber weighted base. (6) The boot is a plain black cylinder with ring lines and no moulded detail.
suggestions: Fix the flag colours: fluorescent red-orange (linear ~0.95,0.18,0.05) and off-white (0.85), roughness 0.7, plus a nylon weave normal map. Remove the stray white dots (check the UV seams or the dot decal).
Reuse the improved flag cloth poses from the pro flag (limp, breeze, wind variants with gravity sag and a curled edge).
Grassroots wear: a slight bend of 1-3° in the pole, faded yellow (desaturate 15%), black tape wraps, scratches, and mud and grass stains on the bottom 300 mm. One 256x1024 strip texture.
Replace the brown disc with either nothing (pole pushed into turf with a small flattened-grass decal) or a black rubber weighted base (Ø 300 mm, 40 mm, moulded grip ribs).
Keep total cost under ~800 tris with a shared small atlas.
renderer_notes: The lawn and sky are renderer/ground. The flag's backlit side looks darker partly because there is no transmission in the shader.

summary: The main building close-up is a black box with flat window-grid texture, random beige rectangles and evenly spaced fins. It has no depth, entrance or signage, and is half hidden behind oversized birch leaf cards.
critique: The close-up shows a 3-storey curtain-wall building with vertical black fins, white spandrel bands, a cyan accent line at the parapet and a projecting black-clad block. The aerial shows a few plain flat-roofed boxes and a white barrel-vault indoor hall. Problems: (1) The glazing is opaque near-black with beige and white rectangles scattered at random (blinds or lit rooms?) that read as texture noise. There are no mullions or transoms with depth, no glass reflection, no interior parallax, no frit or solar control tint, and no reveal between glass and spandrel. (2) The fins are uniform thin black slats at regular spacing with no fixing brackets, no variation and no shadow depth. (3) The black panels of the projecting block are featureless rectangles with thin outlines. (4) There is no visible entrance, canopy, doors, club crest or signage, and no plinth detail or drainage channel at the base. The building meets the paving with a thin beige upstand only. (5) The roofs, seen from the air, are flat grey with no plant, rooflights, PV or parapet capping detail, which is why the buildings read as boxes. (6) The indoor dome is a plain white barrel shape with a dark roof stripe, but a real superclub indoor pitch building has ribbed cladding, gable glazing and doors. (7) For a superclub the main building is small and generic. Real first-team buildings (for example Carrington and Cobham) are long, low, highly articulated pavilions with large glazed atria, timber or stone cladding, landscaped forecourts and drop-off. (8) The birch leaves in the foreground are 15-25 cm flat cards and dominate the frame, which is a vegetation issue but hurts this view badly.
suggestions: Rebuild the curtain wall as geometry plus a trim sheet: 50 mm deep mullions every 1.5 m and transoms at floor lines (box strips, ~12 tris each), glass panes set 60 mm back, glass material with roughness 0.05, metallic 0, slight blue-green tint, and a cheap interior-mapping or cube-map 'room' shader so floors read through. Replace the random beige rectangles with a coherent blinds/occupancy mask on 20-30% of panes.
Fins: vary depth (150-300 mm), add brackets at each floor and a slight colour/roughness variation. Cast real shadows on the glass by setting them 200 mm proud.
Add a main entrance: a 3-4 m deep cantilevered canopy, a double-height glazed atrium with revolving/sliding doors, a club crest and lettering on the canopy fascia, a drop-off lay-by and bollards.
Roofscape: parapet copings, plant enclosures with louvres, rooflights, PV arrays and a few vents. These are cheap boxes and make the aerial read as real buildings.
Material variety: one or two cladding materials besides black glass (timber rainscreen, light stone or brick plinth), a 300-600 mm plinth, and rain staining under copings.
Indoor hall: add standing-seam ribbed normal map, gable-end glazing band, roller doors and a plant room annex.
Scale the birch leaves down to ~6-8 cm and cluster them on twigs (or use more, smaller leaf cards). Keep foreground trees from blocking the hero building view in the review camera.
renderer_notes: No reflections makes all glazing render as flat black. Even a single sky reflection probe would lift the facades considerably.

summary: A convincing layout (solar canopies over bays, landscaped islands, lamp columns, varied car colours and body styles), but the surfacing has a hard two-tone seam, the cars are simplified, and the canopies and bays lack detail.
critique: The car park reads well as a modern training-ground staff car park: long rows of bays under PV canopies, a central aisle, lamp columns, shrub islands, trees beyond, and cars in a believable spread of colours and segment types (SUVs, saloons, hatchbacks). Problems: (1) The surfacing switches abruptly from light grey concrete on the left aisle to dark asphalt on the right along a straight diagonal edge, which looks like two un-blended materials. There are no kerbs, drainage gullies, tyre wear or oil staining in the bays, and no patch repairs. (2) The bay markings are crisp perfect white bars with no wear, no arrows or text, and no disabled or EV bays. (3) The cars are low-detail: smooth bodies with soft lamp shapes, little panel definition, wheels a little small and set in shallow arches. At distance they read OK, but up close they look toy-like (the near black SUV and white saloon). The white saloon sits slightly askew and nose-out into the aisle. (4) The PV canopies are flat slabs on round posts, without purlins, panel grid, cable trays, under-canopy lighting or EV chargers, which a superclub canopy would have. (5) The lamp columns are thin and generic. There are no signage, barrier, ticket/ANPR posts or pedestrian walkways.
suggestions: Surfacing: use one asphalt material for the whole park with a separate block-paved or tinted aisle bordered by a 125 mm kerb, a soft blend mask, tyre-track darkening in the bays, oil-drip decals, gullies every ~20 m and a few patch repairs. All decals, ~1 draw call.
Markings: worn thermoplastic lines (edge breakup, 10-20% fade), direction arrows, 'EV' and disabled bay symbols, and hatched walkways. Decals from one 1024 marking atlas.

Canopies: a visible PV panel grid (1.0x1.7 m modules) via normal and albedo, steel purlins beneath, LED strip lights under the canopy, cable trays down two posts, and EV wall-box chargers on every 4th post.

Cars: enlarge the wheels to the correct size (~650-700 mm tyre OD for a C-segment car) with deeper arches, add shut lines and window rubbers via a shared vehicle trim normal map, clearcoat paint with reflection probe, and plates front and rear. Keep 6-10k tris per car LOD0 and impostors beyond 60 m.
Add ANPR camera posts and a rising-arm barrier at the entry, pedestrian zebra crossings to the building, and signage (bay numbers, 'Staff', 'First team').
renderer_notes: No reflections makes car paint and PV glass look matte. A probe or sky reflection would help both.

summary: Pitches with mowing stripes, crisp markings, floodlight columns, ball-stop fencing, goals, mannequins, poles, cones, team shelters and a filming tower make a convincing training complex, but the turf is a flat CG green and the kit is sparse and small.
critique: Good: mow-striped grass with markings, a centre circle and a penalty arc, many pitch floodlight columns, ball-stop fencing behind the goals, full-size goals, a yellow mannequin wall, slalom poles and hurdles, cones, team shelters and a scaffold filming tower (a nice superclub touch). Problems: (1) The turf is a smooth saturated green with even broad stripes. Close up it has no blade texture, no wear (worn goalmouths, centre circle or touchline run-off), no division between pitch and surrounds, and no difference between natural, hybrid and artificial pitches. (2) The pitch looks endless because there is no near-end goal or run-off, and the edges blend into the surrounding lawn without a visible maintained border. (3) The training kit is sparse and tiny at this distance. A superclub session would show clusters of mannequins, rebounders, ball carts with balls, mini-goals, pop-up goals, bibs on a bench, a water/ice bath station and GPS pods. (4) The floodlight columns are thin poles with small heads. Training-pitch columns are typically 15-18 m with 2-4 floodlights on a headframe, and should show bases and access doors. (5) The ball-stop netting is thin vertical lines with no visible net sag or posts with ties.
suggestions: Turf material: a tileable 1024-2048 grass albedo and normal with blade detail, plus a mowing-stripe mask that changes roughness and brightness, not only colour. Add a wear mask (goalmouths, centre spot, along touchlines) with thinner, browner, rougher turf and a few divot decals.
Pitch surrounds: a 3-6 m run-off in slightly different turf, a perimeter path, and a low pitch-side barrier or rope-and-post line, so each pitch reads as a distinct prepared surface.

Populate sessions: 2-3 prop clusters per pitch drawn from the kit library (mini-goals, rebounder, ball cart with 15-20 instanced balls, mannequin wall, pole slalom, agility ladder, bib pile on a bench, cool-box and water bottles). All instanced, under ~20k tris per cluster.
Floodlights: 15-18 m columns with a tapered profile (Ø ~200 mm base to ~100 mm top), base plate and door, a 2-4-lamp headframe with visors aimed at the pitch.
Ball-stop netting: posts every 5 m with a visible top cable and a sagging net (alpha-tested net texture on a lightly curved strip), 6-8 m high behind the goals.
renderer_notes: The shadow of an off-camera object on the pitch at left looks like a floating shadow. Check what casts it. The flat turf shading is partly the lack of AO and grazing-angle specular.

summary: A sensible overall layout (main building, car parks, multiple pitches, indoor hall, access road, perimeter fence in farmland), but the landscape is a flat patchwork of untextured fields with isolated lollipop trees, and the site lacks the bunding, screening belts and density of a real superclub ground.
critique: Good: the access road leads to a drop-off and car parks next to the main building, about 8-10 pitches sit in a grid with paths between them, an indoor hall with a big full-size pitch footprint, a maintenance yard, a fenced perimeter and surrounding farmland with hedgerows. Problems: (1) The terrain is completely flat. Real training grounds sit on gently undulating land with landscaped earth bunds (2-5 m) around the perimeter for privacy and noise, and drainage ditches and attenuation ponds. (2) The trees are isolated, similar-sized lollipops spaced evenly along lines. There are no dense woodland belts or screening shelterbelts around the perimeter (Cobham, Carrington and Finch Farm all hide behind thick planting), no copses, and no understorey. (3) The farmland is flat-coloured rectangles with uniform tone, with no crop rows, tramlines or field texture, and the hedgerows are thin dark lines without width. (4) The site is sparse: big empty lawn areas between buildings, no gatehouse or security lodge, no maintenance compound with machinery sheds, no groundsman's nursery or turf store, no staff and visitor paths, and no attenuation pond. (5) The close-range vegetation cards (birch leaves) are oversized, and the oak canopies are blobby clusters that read as clipart. (6) The perimeter fence and security line is barely visible.
suggestions: Terrain: add a low-frequency heightfield (±1-2 m over 200 m) and perimeter bunds 3-4 m high with 1:3 slopes, planted with dense woodland, with pitches set on terraced level platforms with small banks between them.

Planting: perimeter woodland belts 15-30 m deep made of instanced tree clusters (mixed oak, birch, alder) with a shrub understorey. Vary tree scale ±30% and break the regular spacing with Poisson-disc sampling. Use HLOD/impostor cards beyond 150 m.

Farmland: field textures with crop rows and tramlines (oriented per field), a few fields in stubble or ploughed, hedgerows 1.5-2.5 m wide as volumetric strips with hedgerow trees, and field-gate gaps.

Fill the site program: a gatehouse with barrier and ANPR on the access road, a maintenance compound (machinery shed, fuel store, spoil heaps, turf nursery), an attenuation pond with reeds, footpaths linking building to pitches with lighting bollards, and a small spectator mound by the academy pitch.
Leaf card scale: birch leaves ~5 cm, oak ~10 cm, grouped on twig cards. Add a second LOD with clustered leaf billboards so mid-distance canopies are not blobs.
renderer_notes: The distance haze is reasonable. The flat farmland colour is partly the ground shader's tiling, not only the layout.
